objectives.text: Explain why 1/t is proportional to the initial rate in the thiosulfate–starch clock method and the conditions this requires.
Interpret the ln(1/t) against ln[I<sup>−</sup>] plots to deduce reaction orders, and justify holding ionic strength constant with KCl.
Calculate the rate constant from the standard-run timing, thiosulfate amount and initial concentrations, accounting for the reaction stoichiometry.
Justify deriving the activation energy from a plot of ln(1/t) against 1/T, and evaluate how timing errors and catalytic impurities affect it.

questions.prompt: In your clock method, why is 1/t proportional to the initial rate?
options: The thiosulfate reacts directly with peroxodisulfate at a rate set by t
The total amount of iodine formed increases in proportion to the time t
The starch complex forms at a rate proportional to the iodide concentration
Each run forms the same fixed amount of iodine, with little reactant consumed
questions.explanation: Because the fixed amount of thiosulfate must be used up before colour appears, every run forms the same amount of iodine, so rate ≈ amount/t, provided only a small fraction (about 2.5%) of peroxodisulfate reacts. Thiosulfate reacts with iodine, not with peroxodisulfate.

questions.prompt: Your clock method treats 1/t as proportional to the initial rate. Which statements describe conditions this relies on?
options: Only a small fraction of peroxodisulfate reacts before the colour appears
The iodine formed must accumulate freely as tri-iodide during timing
Thiosulfate must be in excess over peroxodisulfate throughout the run
The colour appears almost instantly once thiosulfate is exhausted
The reaction must be first order in thiosulfate
The same fixed amount of thiosulfate is used in every run
questions.explanation: A fixed thiosulfate amount means each time t marks the same iodine formed; only about 2.5% of peroxodisulfate reacted, and the colour delay is short. Thiosulfate in excess would stop the blue colour ever appearing, so the clock would never run.

questions.prompt: Your ln(1/t) against ln[I<sup>−</sup>] plot had a gradient of 1.02 and you made up volumes with KCl. Which statements correctly reflect your reasoning?
options: Without KCl, rising ionic strength would speed up the reaction and inflate the apparent order
The intercept of the log–log plot gives the activation energy directly
The gradient of the log–log plot gives the order with respect to iodide
Ions of the same sign react more slowly as ionic strength increases
KCl was added to keep the total volume constant only, not ionic strength
A gradient near one shows the rate doubles when [I<sup>−</sup>] doubles
questions.explanation: Since 1/t ∝ rate = k[I<sup>−</sup>]<sup>n</sup>…, the log–log gradient is n, so about one means rate doubles with [I<sup>−</sup>]. You used KCl to hold ionic strength constant because the salt effect speeds up reactions between like-charged ions, which would otherwise inflate the orders.

questions.prompt: Suppose you had varied the iodide volume but made up the remaining volume with water instead of KCl. How would your ln(1/t) against ln[I<sup>−</sup>] gradient most likely change?
options: It would exceed one, because water dilutes the thiosulfate and lengthens every time
It would fall below one, because added ionic strength slows reactions between like-charged ions
It would stay at one, because ionic strength affects only the rate constant, not order
It would exceed one, because higher [I<sup>−</sup>] also raises ionic strength and speeds the reaction
questions.explanation: In your report, runs with more KI would also have higher ionic strength, and the primary salt effect speeds reactions between same-sign ions, so 1/t would rise faster than [I<sup>−</sup>] alone predicts, inflating the gradient. Like-charged ions are accelerated, not slowed, by higher ionic strength.

questions.prompt: In your standard run at 295 K, 5.0 × 10<sup>−5</sup> mol of thiosulfate in 50.0 cm<sup>3</sup> was used up in 74 s. Which reasoning correctly gives your rate constant?
options: I<sub>2</sub> formed equals the thiosulfate; rate/([S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>8</sub><sup>2−</sup>][I<sup>−</sup>]) gives 1.7 × 10<sup>−2</sup>
I<sub>2</sub> formed is half the thiosulfate; rate/([S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>8</sub><sup>2−</sup>][I<sup>−</sup>]) gives 8.5 × 10<sup>−3</sup>
I<sub>2</sub> formed is twice the thiosulfate; rate/([S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>8</sub><sup>2−</sup>][I<sup>−</sup>]) gives 3.4 × 10<sup>−2</sup>
I<sub>2</sub> formed is half the thiosulfate; rate/[I<sup>−</sup>]<sup>2</sup> gives 4.2 × 10<sup>−3</sup>
questions.explanation: Each I<sub>2</sub> consumes two S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup>, so 2.5 × 10<sup>−5</sup> mol I<sub>2</sub> formed, giving 6.8 × 10<sup>−6</sup> mol dm<sup>−3</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>. Dividing by 0.0200 × 0.0400 gives 8.5 × 10<sup>−3</sup>. Your measured orders, not the 2I<sup>−</sup> stoichiometry, set the rate equation, so dividing by [I<sup>−</sup>]<sup>2</sup> is wrong.

questions.prompt: Your standard run at 295 K gave k = 8.5 × 10<sup>−3</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup> dm<sup>3</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>. Which statements about this calculation are correct?
options: The initial rate equals the moles of thiosulfate divided by 74 s
Doubling the thiosulfate volume would roughly double the calculated k
The iodine concentration formed by the colour change was 5.0 × 10<sup>−4</sup> mol dm<sup>−3</sup>
Each mole of iodine formed consumes one mole of peroxodisulfate
The units of k follow from the reaction being second order overall
The rate is divided by [I<sup>−</sup>]<sup>2</sup> because the equation contains two iodide ions
questions.explanation: Half of 5.0 × 10<sup>−5</sup> mol thiosulfate gives 2.5 × 10<sup>−5</sup> mol I<sub>2</sub> in 50.0 cm<sup>3</sup>, i.e. 5.0 × 10<sup>−4</sup> mol dm<sup>−3</sup>. Your experimental rate equation, not the stoichiometry, sets the divisor [S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>8</sub><sup>2−</sup>][I<sup>−</sup>]. Doubling thiosulfate doubles t, leaving k unchanged.

questions.prompt: Your Arrhenius plot of ln(1/t) against 1/T gave E<sub>a</sub> = 53 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>. Which statements about this derivation and its errors are correct?
options: Using 1/t works because 1/t is proportional to k when concentrations are fixed
A ±1 s timing error matters most at 325 K, where t is only 10 s
The gradient of the plot equals −E<sub>a</sub>/R, independent of the fixed amount of thiosulfate
Catalytic impurities shorten times but cannot change the gradient of the plot
Timing errors matter most at 285 K, because longer times accumulate more error
Using 1/t instead of k changes the gradient, so E<sub>a</sub> is only approximate
questions.explanation: With identical mixtures at every temperature, 1/t is proportional to k, so constants only shift the intercept and the gradient still gives −E<sub>a</sub>/R. A ±1 s error is proportionally largest at the 10 s run. Impurities that shorten some runs unevenly can distort the gradient.

questions.prompt: Suppose trace Cu<sup>2+</sup> contamination shortened only your 285 K runs. How would this most likely affect the activation energy from your ln(1/t) against 1/T plot?
options: It would be too low, because the low-temperature point rises and flattens the gradient
It would be unchanged, because 1/t stays proportional to k at each temperature
It would be unchanged, because a catalyst shifts every ln(1/t) value equally
It would be too high, because the low-temperature point rises and steepens the gradient
questions.explanation: A shorter 285 K time raises ln(1/t) at the largest 1/T, making the gradient less negative, so −gradient × R gives a smaller E<sub>a</sub>. Contamination confined to one temperature cannot shift every point equally.
